utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. Before we continue the examination of Mr. Djeric, I'd like to deal with a few procedural matters. First of all I would like to deliver a decision on the Defence request that the Trial Chamber call an additional witness pursuant to Rule 98. This is a decision on the Defence request that the Trial Chamber call an additional witness pursuant to Rule 98. On the 15th of June 2006, the Trial Chamber announced that it intended to call some of the participants in the so-called bridge negotiations in the municipality of Bosanski Novi. This referred to four persons mentioned by Witness Radomir Pasic in private session on the 15th of December 2005, who, according to Pasic, could corroborate his testimony regarding the negotiations between the Muslim representatives, the Serb authorities, and international organisations in Bosanski Novi in May, June, and July 1992. The Trial Chamber announced that it did not intend to call all four persons. On the 20th of June, a legal officer of the Chamber contacted three of the persons referred to by Witness Pasic for whom contact details had been found. All three persons expressed willingness to testify. On the 21st of June the Trial Chamber stated that it had decided to call two of the bridge negotiators, Amir Delic, who came to testify on the 27th of June, and Emin Puric, who testified on the 11th of July, yesterday. In its request, the Defence argues that the third person contacted on the 20th of June should be called as a Chamber witness as well, since, as the Defence put it, he has no real connection with Mr. Delic or presumably Mr. Puric, while Delic and Puric are, according to the Defence, friends. Another reason the Defence considers relevant is that the third person not only lives but also works in Bosanski Novi today. In its response, the Prosecution argues that the expected evidence of the third bridge negotiator concerns, in essence, the question whether the departure of non-Serbs from Bosanski Novi was voluntary but that Trial Chamber has heard sufficient evidence to be able to make findings concerning this question as well as whether crimes were carried out in the municipality during the relevant time. The Trial Chamber based its decision to call Mr. Delic and Mr. Puric to testify on the understanding that they were the two main negotiators at the incidents in question. This information was obtained from the conversation held with those two persons on the 20th of June and was reiterated by Mr. Delic during his testimony. Mr. Puric described himself as the person who coordinated the negotiation team and stated that he and Mr. Delic were in practically all the negotiations. The Defence's argument for calling the third person contacted on the 20th of June are speculative. The Defence suggests that presumed differences in certain circumstances of the third person make his testimony more credible, worthwhile and indispensable, but this is mere speculation. The fact that the Chamber has heard two leading figures in the negotiations and that their testimonies have been subjected to cross-examination by both parties means that this area which does not concern acts or conduct of the accused, has been sufficiently covered and tested. Moreover, considering the range of testimonies and material already in evidence regarding the events in Bosanski Novi, the Chamber finds that it has now received sufficient evidence about events in that municipality. The Trial Chamber therefore denies the Defence request. This concludes the Trial Chamber's decision. There is another matter that needs our attention and that is concern expressed by Mr. Krajisnik on the transcript of the 20th of June 2006. Reference was made to his testimony in a question put to Mr. Krajisnik on the 21st of June. The English transcript has been officially corrected. The checking and the correction of page 2645 [sic] on the 20th of June 2006, has been done as promised on the 21st of June, and it is now accepted by the Chamber on the one hand that on the 21st of June, at page 26187, Mr. Harmon cited entirely accurately from the erroneous English transcript as it then stood. But on the other hand, that Mr. Krajisnik had been entirely correct in his recollection of his own evidence from the previous day and in his refusal to accept that what was being put to him by Mr. Harmon, that refusal was correct. When I am referring to the -- these pages, a review and correction was done on lines 1 to 9 and lines 13 to 19 of page 26045. This concludes the procedural issues. Could we then ask you, Mr. Usher, to escort Mr. Djeric into the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one of the few words I even understand in your language. Mr. Djeric, I'd first like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that in mid-March, 1992, you were -- you became the Prime Minister designate of the Bosnian Serb republic. When did you -- do you remember when you exactly became the Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I do hear you say Bosnia-Herzegovina but I think we are now talking about the Bosnian Serb republic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the actual terms or actually the dates but I think it was sometime in mid-March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, why were you selected to -- for this post?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I assume it was for professional reasons, as an economist, as a person who was not an activist in the earlier period, or someone who was involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know who selected you or who approached you to take up that post?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was, as far as I can remember, Biljana Plavsic who nominated me at the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But usually before being publicly announced in an assembly and proposed, some contact is made with the candidate. Do you remember who approached you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was probably the case that there was some contacts but this is not something that I particularly remember. I know that before that, in that time, I was -- I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how was your appointment formalised? You were proposed, as you said, in the assembly session, as far as you remember, by Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then who finally took the decision to appoint you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly did, a body of the assembly, representatives of the Serbian people in the assembly, and this was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Representatives of the assembly, or the deputies of the Serbian people in the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They comprised the Assembly of the Serbian People at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And they decided that you would be the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, then, once you had become a Prime Minister, what steps did you take to set up an office, an administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I began to have regular contacts with ministers or deputy ministers in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who were representatives of the Serbian people, and who were nominated to that body of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I had contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us, in your office, in your -- in your Prime Minister's office, how many people were employed and did you select them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have an office, because when I was nominated as Prime Minister designate, I was still a member of the government, I was a minister in the government of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said yesterday that I was a minister without portfolio or actually it was called minister for development, because I dealt with the matters relating to development. I didn't have an office. I was in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and I had an office there. But I worked a little bit on these tasks also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But later on, when you were not functioning any more as a minister in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, how many staff did you have available once you were in Pale, once you were functioning in Pale?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the operations began, after the first conflicts broke out, there were a number of them. They were arriving, all of these cadres that I talked about. They were either ministers or deputy ministers or assistant ministers in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the makeup, more or less, of the future government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And support staff in your office, how many people were supporting you, who didn't hold any formal position as a minister or a deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several people. Mostly these were people from the government down there, namely Sarajevo, and there, they performed the same duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many approximately?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially perhaps when I add them all up, there were perhaps ten people, including drivers and other staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What resources --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how did that develop over the time you held the position? When you resigned, how many were there approximately in your Prime Minister's office?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministries had fewer staff members, but there were people -- I mean, I don't know exactly how many. Maybe ten or more ministries, so then if we say that they had an average of ten people, up to ten people, then, yeah, that would be all right. It depends -- of course the ministry for internal affairs had many more staff members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was focusing on your office, your office of the Prime Minister, so not support staff in the other ministries but just who supported your work.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, I didn't understand. In my office, there was a secretary, a woman, and there was also a male secretary, the vice-president was there, and maybe two other people. That was the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What resources were available to you, either in terms of budget or by any other means?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, it was all a little bit disorganised. We were counting on the resources of the municipalities and on the budget of the Serbian Republic and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us exactly what was your role as Prime Minister? What were your tasks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my duty to coordinate the work of the government or the work of the ministries and to deal with the economy, also the legislate you are, to develop the legislature, the rules of the game, to establish institutions, all those duties that are carried out by a government usually. We started from scratch, as they say, so it was necessary to go about creating all these things slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said that it was your duty to coordinate the work of the government or the work of the ministries, and to deal with the economy. Was there not a Minister of Economy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking generally about the government. There was a minister for the economy but I am talking about a government priority. It was one of the government priorities to start up production and manufacture. There is no future without production. So this was a priority. But of course this was something that was in the domain of the ministry for economic affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, according to the constitution, so I'm thinking in terms of the legal framework, how were the ministers of the government selected and appointed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were simply taken from the previous government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were government ministers in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina or their deputies or their assistants who were proposed from the ranks of the Serbian people and they joined the new government, except in a few cases, in some cases where the Serbian people, for example, did not have their own minister or some assistant ministers did not appear, in such cases other candidates were proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I asked you specifically how this was done under the constitution. What does the constitution say about selection of ministers and appointment of ministers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution, the Prime Minister-designate proposes certain candidates to the assembly and that is how they are appointed. In this case, in the beginning, according to a decision, people were assigned. There was a combined approach. There was a decision of the Supreme Defence Council or the Security Council for security that people who were part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina government should join this new government, and I have to say that before there was a ministerial council of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and these ministers were in that council, the ministers that we are talking about, so these ministers simply then joined the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question would you, especially those ministers who had not yet functioned in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina before, who suggested or who proposed them to become members of the -- of the ministerial council of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prime Minister-designate initially, or later, if we were just filling in certain posts, this was then done by the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it was you personally who made these suggestions, the proposals for --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put forward proposals but this was at the suggestion of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who or what body in the party would suggest to you what ministers to propose for appointment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the party. These were his proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to go back a few lines but we are not sure that the witness actually mentioned the Supreme Defence Council. Perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll clarify that. There seems to be -- your suspicion is that there is a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's what we think is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I read to you -- I'll read to you part of your answer as it was translated to us in English and I'd like you to verify whether that's what you said in your own language. I'll read from the transcript: "In this case, in the beginning -- no, no. Let me -- you said there was a combined approach. There was a decision of the Supreme Defence Council or the Security Council for security that people who were part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina government should join the new government." The issue is whether you mentioned here the Supreme Defence Council or the Security Council for security. Is that what you said or did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is not the Supreme Defence Council here. It's the National Council for Security. That's what it was called. The Council for National Security. That has nothing to do with the Supreme Defence Council. It's a party body more than anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the suggestions made by this party body, was that something we would find in the constitution or was it something informal or practical? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was more a question of the practical implementation of policies. As I said, I wasn't really -- I didn't have any function in the party so I wasn't really aware of all of these details. I didn't know anything about the party structure or anything that had to do with that particular aspect of policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I take it that you knew the ministers who had served with you on the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you give us a few examples of those who did not and you're perhaps unfamiliar with?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that I didn't know were Mico Stanisic, Minister of Police, Momcilo Mandic, Minister of Justice; then Subotic, the Defence Minister, I didn't know him earlier, to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you did you inquire into their backgrounds, their qualities, did you form your own opinion on their capacities to become members of what was your government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not at that point in time form an opinion because my hands were tied. These were party nominations, so I practically couldn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain that? I mean, you why the Prime Minister. You said under the constitution it was you who proposed and at the same time you say, well, at least if I understood you well, that your hands were bound, you had to follow suggestions made by party organs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply couldn't put forward anyone who was not from that potential cadre pool allocated by the party. People were in a way put forward for the post of minister, and all I had to do was to formally nominate them. I didn't know too many people either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was, if I understand your testimony well, it was the party rather than you who decided who would become a minister.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The party made the decisions. All I did was to put people forward. I was in the role of the formal nominator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to move to another subject. Could you tell us, until when exactly you did remain Prime Minister of the Bosnian Serb republic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until October 9th, 1993 [as interpreted]. That was when I resigned, if I remember correctly, the 9th of October. That was the assembly in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us for what reasons you resigned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason for my resignation, generally speaking, was because the authorities or the government was not functioning. The party structure outweighed the rule of law aspect of the state, let's say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give an example of that, an occasion where you felt that it was the party structure rather than the legal structure of the state that was decisive?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ministers would be in the circle of the party president. Everything would happen there. The government was simply marginalised. It was on the brink of what was going on. We were busy, and all our initiatives about laws, drafts, certain procedures, seemed to be impeded at some point. They were blocked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us, as I asked before, could you give us an example of something you would have liked to do which was, as you said, blocked or where you felt that you were impeded at some point to do what you had in mind or what the government had in mind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the replacement of certain ministers, primarily the Minister of Internal Affairs and Minister of Justice, that simply wasn't going through. Secondly, I asked for a procedure to be put in place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please finish this portion of your answer. You asked for a procedure to be put in place for what?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To have procedures put in place in relation to possible crimes, to establish what a crime is, and then to deal with such matters, to process these matters. This would then simply come to a stop and I wasn't -- I was unable to do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just first focus on the first part of your answer. You said, for example, the replacement of certain ministers, and my question was where you felt that you were blocked in doing what you had in mind. Do I have to understand this, that you had in mind to replace certain ministers and you mentioned the Minister of Internal Affairs and the Minister of Justice, did you have that in mind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who blocked you? Who blocked you to do so?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the party was the one who did the blocking, first of all, but I didn't really find any understanding with the others either. It all centred on President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The second part of your answer was that you had in mind to put procedures in place in relation to possible crimes, to establish what a crime is and then to deal with such matters, to process these matters. Why did you feel the need to put procedures in place to that end?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply thought, well, I'm not a lawyer, I don't know what a crime is and what it isn't. So starting from the idea that we needed to act preventively, that certain boundaries had to be crossed and that we needed to have our own position on this matter, these two ministries were key ministries in that sense, and the government on several occasions adopted a conclusion on the responsibility in that sphere of the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Internal Affairs, for us to receive information, simply to know what's what. You know, I don't know. All I can do is set out from the idea that the government was there either to prevent something from happening or to process something if it did occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What caused the concern that you had that the government had to deal with what crime was and how crime should be prevented or processed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply my responsibility in this respect. You see, I didn't want to be taken by surprise. I didn't want things to go apart from the government. I told you already that the government had been sidelined. I didn't want things to happen without us having taken a stand with regard to these questions. You know the way it is. There is always some kind of whispering, some kind of rumours, and so on and so forth. So I really don't know what is what, you see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What were these whispers and rumours about? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean quite simply, I mean, from the very outset, you had conflicts, you see. It is possible that there were some transgressions. I don't know. Well, if things like that happen, then the appropriate ministries have to react. Furthermore, for example, I would hear of a case in Sarajevo, in Grbovica, in the area where the Serbs lived, well, I would receive information through private channels, you see, that a person was creating certain problems and so on and so forth, with some person nicknamed Batica, I think. When I heard about that, I did my best, after, well, quite a bit of resistance, you see, on the part of these ministries. They didn't want to detain that individual. Things like that. Quite simply, I did my best so that the rule of law would be felt on the ground so that the judiciary would work. I wanted to have cases tried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the information you received through whatever channels, private or not, limited to what happened in Sarajevo? You specifically mentioned Grbovica. Or did it go beyond that geographical area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, specifically this has to do with that particular case but I simply proceeded from the fact that there were conflicts everywhere, Bijeljina, Zvornik, from the very outset, and these questions have to be dealt with, you see. In this respect, I encountered certain problems with the very top of the Serb republic, specifically with Karadzic, because he thought that this could be dealt with later. Do you understand that? And I asked for this to be done immediately. This very top -- well, quite simply, it's not that crimes as such were justified but with regard to the timing of prosecutions, there was some procrastination or some tolerance, if I can put it that way, but I wanted to have things dealt with immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you're using the name, the very top, the expression, "The very top," and you then said specifically with Karadzic. Was Karadzic, in your experience, the only one who took that position or was this -- was the top in this respect broader?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'm primarily referring to him because he was the most explicit in this regard. He was. Others in a way, well, were, well, sort of more passive in that respect. He was explicit. He thought that this could be dealt with later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when you talk about others who were more passive, could you tell us who you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I mean, objectively speaking, I mean I'm referring to the entirety of, well, there was this conflict between, say, the Prime Minister and conditionally speaking the very top. Well, it started from the very first days, in respect of the work of the government, the party structure, a state based on the rule of law, and people would usually tend to stick with those who were in charge, but, well, you know, the other people, well, there was a certain lack of criticism, if I can put it that way. A lack of a critical attitude. Well, I mean, they tended to go along with this view that these possible crimes could be dealt with later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You've not answered my question yet. Apart from what you said you're referring to the entirety. The entirety of what? Could I just, for example, would that include Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Koljevic too. Well, roughly, say there were five of us, and well, more or less, always a session would end with a ratio of three to two. Biljana Plavsic and I were on one side and the three of them were on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're talking about the five of you and you're talking about sessions. Could you be a bit more specific? The five of you, you mentioned yourself and Mrs. Plavsic. The three of them would be the three of what exactly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you say, "Of us", your answer seems to take it for granted that there were five. Why specifically these five? What does mean in this respect "us"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean it was some kind of a coordinating body which in a state of war was supposed to be called the Presidency. Well, in a state of war. But a state of war had never been declared. There was only a state of immediate threat of war that had been declared so then there was this sort of coordinating body which was convened by the president of the party, Karadzic, and then before it would be the two members of the Presidency, Koljevic and Biljana, who were members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I, as Prime Minister, and Krajisnik as president of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say a coordinating body, and you say it was supposed to be called the Presidency in a state of war but there was no state of war. Could you describe to us whether this coordinating body functioned similar to how a Presidency would be functioning if a state of war would have been declared or were there differences?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did not actually function because, well, the way I understood things, that was one of the problems too. The top people, those people who were supposed to be in charge of that body would be Koljevic or Mrs. Plavsic because they were the members of the Presidency before the war. You see? So there was this lingering conflict, whether Koljevic or Plavsic or Radovan Karadzic should be in charge of that body. And in that conflict of theirs, well, it was the president of the party who handled it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But now, the -- as you said the coordinating body. Explain to us what the situation was. But if you would have considered how you thought a Presidency in a state of declared war would function compared to how this coordinating body in fact functioned, apart from disagreements on perhaps on who should be in charge but the practical functioning of what you considered to be appropriate in a state of war, and how it -- this coordinating body actually functioned, was there a difference? Was it the same? If there was a difference, what would be the difference?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand what you were saying. What do you mean by this difference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to find out from what I understand within the legal framework, if a state of war would have been declared, then there should have been a Presidency expanded by the Prime Minister and the president of the assembly. That's how this Chamber understood the evidence before it. Now, there was only a state of imminent threat of war, and you're talking about a coordinating body, and you mentioned five persons, three members of the Presidency, the Prime Minister and the president of the assembly. So in the composition of that coordinating body, and the composition of what would have been a Presidency once a state of war would have been declared was actually the same. Now, I'm asking myself, and I'm asking you, as a matter of fact, whether the functioning of this coordinating body differed from what you would have expected a Presidency in a state of war, comprised of the same persons, how that would have functioned.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, there should have been a difference. You see, I mean, formally it's the same people, the same persons, but my understanding of the law is that it would only be natural for this Presidency to be chaired by one of the members of the pre-war Presidency. I mean those who were members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say Plavsic or Koljevic because they were directly elected by the people, and they were in executive positions whereas Karadzic was only president of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you said that it's how it should have been but that wasn't the way it was. The actual situation, the five, as you said, "us," did that function according to how you would expect a Presidency, a five-persons Presidency in a state of war, would have functioned?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, well, I've already told you. I mean, it should have been different. It should have been the members of the Presidency. It should have been chaired either by Koljevic or Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. You explained to us that the members of the Bosnian Serb Presidency were Karadzic, Plavsic, Koljevic. You also told us about the five. Would -- who was normally attending the meetings of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I was present perhaps in 50 per cent of all situations, you see. Everybody came there. Well, as the president deemed necessary, often even his wife was there. Sometimes some other persons would attend, persons who would be invited. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were there members not -- were there persons who attended those meetings on a regular basis, that is frequently, who were not specifically invited for the occasion but attended the meetings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my domain, well, from the point of view of my own domain I could not have known who was invited and who was not invited, but there were people outside this circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did they always or almost always or now and then or frequently attend? Could you give us an impression of those --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, when invited, sometimes they would invite experts, sometimes they would invite lawyers, sometimes they would invite, well, sometimes a military man would be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you were talking about the five, "us,", were they usually attending the meetings of the Presidency and you mentioned them, that is apart from Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, yourself, and you said already that I think that you said that in 50 per cent you would attend, and the last person you mentioned, Mr. Krajisnik, was he usually attending the Presidency meetings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How often did the Presidency meet, Presidency meetings where you and, as you just told us, Mr. Krajisnik, would often attend?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I've said that perhaps I attended about 50 per cent. I mean, I did. Krajisnik was there too -- well, actually I didn't really understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, how often did you meet -- but before I go into that any further, let me just -- earlier you said that you resigned in October 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no, no. October 1992. On the 9th of October, 1992. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It appeared in English as 1993 on the transcript, but that has been corrected. All the other questions --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I asked you about meetings of the Presidency in which you attended, Mr. Krajisnik attended, other people attended, was -- were your answers limited to 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of it was limited to 1992. You asked me how often. Well, in the beginning, these sessions were held, well, practically quite often. Sometimes, say, today, and then tomorrow or perhaps in two days. But then as time went by, they did not take place that often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you say not that often, what frequency? Once a week, once every two weeks, two times a week, once a month? Could you give us an indication for the later stages?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the last stage, it was, say, once a week, once fortnightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Who chaired the meetings of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, in the beginning, well, conditionally speaking, there were these clashes, sort of who would be in charge, and for the most part it was Karadzic who chaired the meetings. Well, when I say for the most part, at first there were some misunderstandings and then he took over and then he chaired the meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Who did call the meetings exactly? Who said, "We'll have a meeting tomorrow or next week"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he called the meetings. You see, at first it was some National Security Council and things like that. Well, perhaps -- was it a month and a half, a bit more? Actually, that's what it was, and then it got the contours that I have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This Chamber received evidence that the Presidency was established on the 12th of May 1992. Would you agree with that or would you have another date in mind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that on the 12th of May, there was an assembly session in Banja Luka. I remember that. And believe me, I mean, well, quite simply, as far as these dates are concerned, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the agenda for such Presidency meetings, did you receive an agenda in advance?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, that was usually set at the session itself, usually, and, well, in a way, we asked for this mode of operation to be changed. Quite simply that was Karadzic's nature, that -- I mean, that kind of work was based on his nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you suggested to -- you asked to change this mode of operation. What did you suggest?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, well, a lot of, well, a lot of things as far as the mode of operation was concerned. For example, to schedule meetings on time, to know when meetings would be held, to know what the agenda would be, to know who was invited to attend the meeting. Well, I mean, to improve all of that, you see. But it was very hard. Ultimately I realised that I had -- I have to say that I did not understand who the first man was, and ultimately I understood that the first man was everything. I mean, we insisted, we said things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would suggest something to be put on the agenda, would that receive a positive response?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were minutes distributed to all those who attended the meetings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, minutes, well, you know, at first things were a bit shaky. There were problems with minutes and so on and so forth, the way in which minutes were kept and so on. And -- that was insisted upon, to have minutes written, to have minutes adopted, so that it's not just talk, you see? Well, then, things got a bit better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you receive a copy of the minutes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, well, we got the minutes -- well, it wasn't that it was made for anyone in particular, individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just asking whether you received -- well, some document which were the minutes of that meeting? You said you insisted upon to have minutes written so I understand this to be that they were written down on paper. Did you receive such a document, such a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I mean, well, as far as these minutes are concerned, well, as I was saying, well, it was not easy for us. I know things were improved. I think that some minutes, well, ultimately, well, were being adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, from your recollection, when did you receive the minutes of such meetings, prior to the next one or do you know when and by whom they were prepared?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually we would receive this in some kind of abridged version at the beginning of the next meeting. I mean, well, there weren't any special preparations involved, you know. Since we were all there sort of nearby, a meeting would be called sort of please come, well, say, when the meeting would start, then an abridged version of the minutes of the previous meeting would be looked at and then we'd move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did those who occasionally attended the meetings, those who were invited, you said sometimes even a military or an expert, are you aware of them receiving copy of the minutes as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot assert anything. I cannot say yes or no. Well, they were at the meeting so they could have been made aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, were these minutes, you said, "adopted," I think. Were they signed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not signed at that time. I assumed that they were signed later when they were archived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there a possibility to -- or did you or did the meeting review the minutes they had received from the previous -- one of the previous sessions, was there any discussion about, "This is not reflecting" or "this perfectly reflects what we discussed last time"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because simply these minutes were very brief, on a piece of paper. They could not really reflect all of the talks. It was more in the form of notes of a meeting. It wasn't a proper record of a meeting. It was a record with just very brief notes, the agenda and what was discussed or what the conclusions were, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This brings me -- you said what the conclusions were. Could you tell us in what way were conclusions adopted during these sessions? I mean, was there a vote, was there -- I take it from your previous answer, matters were discussed and you said these discussions were not reflected in the minutes but as you said, it wasn't a proper record but it was the agenda and what was discussed and what the conclusions were. How were conclusions adopted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no voting, simply speaking. You could see who was for and who was against. I said earlier that in most cases, and on all issues, Biljana Plavsic and I were in a minority, in a way. You could simply note that. There was no need for a vote. I don't remember. Perhaps there was a vote but I'm just saying that that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if there had been a majority, and a minority, as far as conclusions were concerned and where you said there may not have been a vote, how did you find this in the minutes later on? Did you find that as a conclusion adopted or was it stated that it was a split decision or --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't something that was on the basis of split opinions. The president simply thought that in time of war, it should not be like that. It should not be said that there were any divisions, there should be no sign of that. There was simply a statement such and such a conclusion was made, this and this was resolved. So it was never actually recorded who was in favour and who was against.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said that it was usually three against two. Do you remember occasions where Mr. Krajisnik was a minority who was overruled -- was in a minority or perhaps was a minority that was overruled by a majority?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember anything like that happening. For the most part, Krajisnik was -- he had no reserves about the opinions of Karadzic, and Koljevic would usually take their side, the side of those two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another subject. Could you tell us how the Presidency communicated with the government and perhaps governmental organs? Did the Presidency receive reports from the government? Did the government receive reports from the Presidency? How was the communication? What happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communication generally was very bad, and I said that before, because of the position of the government and its views. Karadzic considered himself to be the government, that he was the be-all, and that in a way it was not permitted that the government works properly, that it establishes a legal basis, and it acts according to the rule of law. Simply, it was the concept of a party state, and that was the biggest problem of that government, conditionally speaking. The government didn't have any opposition. Had there been an opposition, things would have been different. According to what he thought, the government was there just as a kind of technical attachment, not a body that should create policies, in a way. I had problems the entire time, because the government was uninformed about policies, strategies, about the current situation. So can you imagine a government operating in such conditions? The legislature could not be established, never mind any other things. I don't know if I need to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this moment. I'd like to take you back to two of your previous answers, one being how conclusions were adopted and another one on an example you gave on the government obstructed in paying proper attention to the definition of crimes, how to prevent or how to process crimes. Was this discussed at any Presidency meeting you attended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I had the impression that you actually put more than one question to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I referred to two of your previous answers, one about your concerns that the government was obstructed in taking proper action, that is defining crimes, et cetera, et cetera, and your answer about how conclusions were adopted at Presidency meetings. I'm asking you whether that concern of the government was ever discussed during a Presidency meeting; that is, how to deal with rumours and perhaps gossip about crimes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did put that question in the context of a state with a rule of law, and I believe that all of these problems, if they did exist, had to be processed. I said earlier that I wanted to deal with this primarily for preventative reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there because what your concern was became clear from your previous answer. What I'd like to know, whether these concerns were discussed in any Presidency meeting you attended.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did open up that question, that this had to be done, but Karadzic was strictly in favour of leaving that for later, that this was something that could be done later. That's where the problem was. It wasn't a question of whether possible crossing of the border should be sanctioned but simply when this had to be done. As the Prime Minister, I wanted this to be taken care of by the two key ministries, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the ministry for justice, and this is where we had these problems within the government and also in communication with the Presidency, with Karadzic, in other words. First of all, with Karadzic because he was the key person there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that Karadzic was very outspoken on this matter and that the others were more passive. Is that what you experienced during such a Presidency meeting or did you experience that outside any of these meetings or sessions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside of the Presidency, I didn't discuss that with anyone else. The question was discussed within the government. There were commissions and groups formed. But then it would stop somewhere. So then I thought that the thing would stop with Karadzic because the ministries and everyone else would need to work, but then it would just stop there. What I'm trying to say is that physically we were separated. The government initially was about a kilometre or two from the Presidency building, and conditionally speaking, then later it was 12 kilometres away from the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you earlier said that Karadzic was very outspoken. I do understand that you discussed the matter in Presidency meetings you attended. You said the others were more passive. Was that a passivity which tended to support your insistence to deal with the matter with criminality very seriously or was it a passivity which would give although passive support to Mr. Karadzic, his preference to delay the matter and not pay attention to it at that moment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a psychologist and I cannot really assess something like that, but if you understand me, this would turn into a conflict between myself, as the Prime Minister, and the president of the party, Mr. Karadzic. It would be a very intense conflict. It would turn into a conflict between me and him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I was asking about the positions taken by the other three. You said they were more passive -- or even passive, I should check there exactly what you said. Let me just find it so that I'm not quoting it in a wrong way. If you give me one second, I'll try to find it, what you exactly said. Yes. You said earlier today, when you were discussing the very top, when you said specifically Karadzic, you said the following: "Well, you see, I'm primarily referring to him because he was the most explicit in this regard. He was. Others in a way, well, were, well, sort of more passive in that respect. He was explicit. He thought that this could be dealt with later." If I analyse your words, it seems that Karadzic was very explicit in dealing with it at a later stage and that the others were more passive, which I did not understand that in this passivity they opposed Karadzic's views but they were not explicit. I'm trying to find out exactly how this went on, what happened in this meeting, where you, as I understand, were in favour of dealing with crime and criminality right away, Mr. Karadzic very much and explicitly opposing to do it at that moment. Could you tell us a bit more in detail what the others said or what made you believe that they were more passive? Did they not say anything at all? How did this happen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said more passive, I simply meant that they were silent during this debate between Karadzic and me on this question. I mean that they didn't have enough -- it's not clear to me. I mean, I cannot know who thought what in their own mind at that time. I cannot even remember specifically the actual situation, and right now I cannot really tell whether this silence on the part of these people was something that was prompted by the actual problem itself or whether it was something that was caused by a standard conflict between myself and Karadzic on many questions, and the attitude to the government in general. So it was just a scene or something that in a way reflected that entire situation. To understand me better, the Presidency didn't feel that it had to keep quiet any crimes, if there were any crimes. It wasn't a question of that, but as I say, there were two lines of thought, whether to do it immediately or whether to process these problems later, and these opinions were expressed by me on one side and Karadzic on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. I have a last question for you, last few questions before we'll have a break. Mr. Djeric, did you attend a meeting in which you received or discussed any reports on an event at a place called Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that. I did request information, requested information, formed commissions, formed groups so that we had information about that. Thus, I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say, "I didn't know about that" and "I did request information," I mean, if you request information on a certain event, there must be a beginning of awareness. I mean, otherwise, you couldn't ask for information. Or is this --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, the entire time, from the beginning, I persisted on the question of rule of law, legal conduct in the field, respecting laws in the field; if it was necessary to process any violations of the law, then that should be done. So simply my manner of work was to form commissions. I did form commissions to find out -- you know, the commissions' work had to do with going around to see the camps, these collection centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll come to that at a later stage but it's not really an answer to my question, because I focused my first question on an event at Koricanske Stijene. You said, "I didn't know about it. I did request information." So there must be a nucleus to say what caused you to ask information.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I requested information pertaining to the reports by world reporters that had to do with the collection centres. That's why I requested information, and a group was formed that would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I was specifically asking about an event at Koricanske Stijene. I don't know whether you are now or were then aware of information, rumours, from whatever source about an event at a place called Koricanske Stijene. Let me perhaps ask you, are you now aware of an event that has taken place at a place called Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know, but to this very day, I don't know what happened there. I just heard about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ask, was this ever subject of discussion or reporting or -- at any Presidency meeting you attended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This was not discussed or reviewed at any meeting, and I never heard of it at any of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break and resume at 25 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly address another procedural matter and perhaps the witness could be kept already standby and to re-enter the courtroom because it will not take more than two or three minutes. I'd like to address the parties regarding exhibits which have been tendered and are still pending admission. During the housekeeping session that was held on the 26th of June, the Prosecution requested additional time to review the exhibits tendered by the Defence during the testimony of Mr. Krajisnik, and to discuss with the Defence any objections they may have. Therefore, the Prosecution's objections were not heard on that day on exhibits D197 through and including D257. Since then the Chamber has heard several Chamber witnesses during whose testimonies additional exhibits have been introduced in court. In total there are now approximately 70 exhibit which are pending admission. The Chamber would like the parties to raise their objections, if any, to these exhibits in writing to be filed no later than Wednesday, the 19th of July 2006. The parties will then have until Friday the 21st of July 2006 to respond in writing to any objections raised by the opposing party. There are a few exhibits which are still missing English translations. All translations must be provided to the registrar no later than this Friday, the 14th of July, 2006. Any exhibits for which we do not have English translations by this date will be denied admission into evidence unless good cause is shown on or before Friday. In such an event, an email to a legal officer of the Chamber copied to the other party will be considered adequate communication. In fulfilling these obligations the parties should refer to exhibit lists which are provided by the registrar. On a related matter, regarding the video which was provided by Chamber witness Amir Delic, on the 27th of June, 2006, the Chamber would like to inform the parties that we are not considering to call for this video into evidence as a Chamber exhibit. Should either of the parties wish to tender it, you're invited to take such action today or tomorrow, even if it's not yet fully translated, then at least the Chamber is informed. This concludes our statement on exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just raise -- there are two points, Mr. Josse would like to raise a supplementary point on another matter that Your Honour has just covered but on the directions Your Honour has just given us to exhibits to be filed next Wednesday and Your Honour has, well, given seven days from today, Your Honour, there is a he real practical problem about that. This Defence team is not actually working after this Friday. We have made our arrangements on that basis and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties can agree on another date, then the Chamber will accept that. But the Chamber is anxious not to end up in a situation where we would be very generous in giving dates and at the same time at a later stage the party might be unhappy that they had no time to -- that at least they were not sufficiently aware of what was in evidence and what was not. And I can tell you that although it was not in what I just said, that although this Chamber also had in mind that we would stop working next -- this Friday, that from the moment you would hear our decision on the matter, you could have concluded that this wish might not have been fully fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore if the parties agree upon another date then the Chamber will seriously consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can see, Your Honour, that it's likely that we are going to be able to sort that out so you can leave it with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll hear from the parties. And then, yes, is that something, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Very briefly we are working on the bridge video. As Your Honour was speaking, I consulted with Mr. Krajisnik about it at the break. We are going to attempt to at least have an extract admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other matter, and that's the Islamic declaration. That was left open after Mr. Subotic's evidence. We are trying to have a portion of that, small portion, translated and admitted into evidence. I will supply the Prosecution with the untranslated portion forthwith, at the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have any comments about its admissibility at this point, but I don't think any translation is necessary. I'm sure the document exists in English and I'm sure for a variety of reasons it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the parties are invited to communicate any knowledge of existing translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you had to wait for a couple of minutes because we had to deal with some procedural matters first. Apologies for that. Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of the Presidency receiving reports from municipal authorities in 1992? Did you ever -- when you were there, did you ever receive any or become aware of reporting by municipal authorities to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This would cover both written and/or oral reports. Would your answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as oral reports are concerned, there were representatives of some municipalities that were sort of milling about. They often came to see Karadzic and Krajisnik on assembly business, especially the Sarajevo municipalities. I saw them often. As for written reports, I don't recall any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now referring to assembly business. My question was mainly about Presidency, reporting to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, well, in both cases. Well, I told you that I don't know about written reports; I mean, I don't remember. Orally, well, I saw people there. Now in what capacity they came and to see who, I don't know. Especially from the Sarajevo municipalities. And even some others, even beyond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give examples of that, and also how you knew that others even beyond the Sarajevo municipalities came to see --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, representatives of Banja Luka came often to have some talks or some contact with Karadzic. Then from Sarajevo municipalities, Vogosca, Ilidza, they were there all the time. How can I know? Say, the Foca municipality. I saw those people there and I assumed that they held certain positions in the municipality but I did not know about that because I was not kept abreast of these contacts or talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your first answer you referred to Karadzic and Krajisnik. You said they often came to see Karadzic and Krajisnik. In your second answer, you said, for instance, representatives of the -- Banja Luka came often to have some talks or some contact with Karadzic. Were you intentionally making that distinction in your first answer where you mainly referred to "especially people from the Sarajevo municipalities," and your second answer going beyond that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somehow the people from the Sarajevo municipalities came to see Krajisnik more often because he is from Sarajevo and he was with them all the time and I assume that these people from Banja Luka and others came to see Karadzic along party lines, along this political party -- I mean, well, I cannot make any assertions to you now. I mean, I cannot tell you anything more reliable on that. I'm sorry. Often there was this conflict between Banja Luka as a centre and Sarajevo as a centre. So they clashed all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us whether Mr. Krajisnik had any particular responsibilities within the -- within the Presidency -- well, let's say within the, as you called them, the five, the -- which you described as a coordinating body consisting of Karadzic, Plavsic, Koljevic, yourself, and Mr. Krajisnik. Did he have any specific -- any particular responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a member of the Presidency by virtue of his office as speaker of the parliament, so that is how he was a member of that body, just like I was there as Prime Minister. That is, as far as the general situation goes. Secondly, I assume that he had quite a few ties to these people. Now, why they came to see him, I don't know that. First of all you should bear in mind that -- well, Karadzic and people around Karadzic, well, that is where the action was. That's where international factors went, international diplomats, military diplomats, international military diplomats. Party people went there. People went there along different lines. That's where the policy making took place. Quite simply, people went there. Now, who played what role, that I cannot tell you specifically, except for the fact that that is where the action was. That is where the centre of all action was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How was Mr. Krajisnik regarded by other members of the Presidency or at least those who attended these meetings of the five? What position did he have in the view of the others, including your view? Not from a formal point of view but what role he played, what his actual position was, because we do understand that since you attended the meetings being the Prime Minister, Mr. Krajisnik attended the meetings being the speaker of the assembly. But in more factual terms.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Krajisnik, well, was considered to be a strong personality. First of all it was the parliament that gave him strength; the parliament, then the party where he had a certain position, and this interpersonal relationship, conditionally speaking this relationship of friendship with Karadzic. I had the feeling, well, that Karadzic trusted only Krajisnik. Now, was that on account of their friendship or was it because he chaired the assembly, I don't know. I cannot make any assertions. These are just my, well -- well, my impressions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further objective basis for those impressions? Any examples of where you remember that the occasion reflected and what you just described as your impression?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, well, I mean, quite simply, conditionally speaking, these were two men in one body, you see? There was very little dissonance there or very little divergence of views. As a matter of fact, I had the impression that Mr. Karadzic considered Mr. Krajisnik to be his very own, private Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I take you to the minutes of the session of the Presidency of the Republika Srpska of the 9th of October 1992? Could the witness be presented with the B/C/S copy of P65, tab 203, tab 3 in this bundle. Mr. Djeric, could you first have a look at this document? You earlier described what you called very brief minutes, not really records but rather reflecting agenda and conclusions. Do you recognise this document as of the kind you described before to us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did they look different, the other ones you described before? I mean what's the difference? What makes you say that this is not the kind of document you described earlier as the minutes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, I mean, even formally I see that there are several conclusions here. You know, that's not the way things were done. There would be a text and then at the end the conclusions would be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's different from what you remember to have received as minutes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I'd like to take you to the top of this document where it says, "Minutes of the session of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, date, 9th of October." It then, two lines further down, reads, "The session was attended by the following members of the Presidency: Momcilo Krajisnik, Dr. Nikola Koljevic, and Dr. Branko Djeric." This was the 9th of October which was, if I understood you well, immediately before your resignation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, well, it doesn't even say where it was held. As far as I know, the 9th of October, as far as I can remember is the day when I resigned, and that was in Prijedor. Do you understand what I'm saying? It doesn't say that it's in Prijedor; again, if I remember correctly. Further on, I see it says present, Krajisnik, Branko Djeric and then there is Koljevic. Now, he's no longer alive so only Krajisnik and I are left. This is a forged document. That can be noticed on the basis of many things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please tell us. If you say -- if you can draw that conclusion on the basis of many things, please tell us what things.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first glance, well, I mean I'd have to read it. I'd have to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take your time, if you need to read it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, quite simply, well, as far as I managed to read this, Boban-Izetbegovic agreement, Boban-Izetbegovic, I don't remember that at all. And then telephone communication with the commander of Slavonski Brod? I mean, you know what? I mean not even in one's wildest dreams, I mean, this simply never happened. And I claim that with full responsibility that this is the first I hear of it. I mean, we never discussed these things at our sessions. No military things. No telephone communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember the last meeting or meetings you had with the -- you earlier said the Presidency or the five where there are only three present here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you were saying. I don't remember. But the session of the Presidency was never held in this capacity. That is what I assert. Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means in the absence of Dr. Karadzic and Dr. Plavsic, you said you never met; the three of you, that is.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Biljana. Never, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes so you say these minutes do not reflect what could have happened according to your recollection, that is a meeting between --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I assert that this is a pure forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand your testimony. So therefore does it make that much sense to ask you about the signature underneath where it reads, "Chaired by Momcilo Krajisnik"? Did Mr. Krajisnik - apart from this meeting, which you say is not a meeting which, in your recollection, ever took place, and could not even have taken place because you never met, the three of you, Krajisnik, you, and Mr. Koljevic - did he ever chair a meeting in the absence of one of the members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, especially that I was considered to be the chairman. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said you never discussed military matters. At the same time earlier in your testimony you said that sometimes military people were invited. What is the use of inviting military people? And we have seen minutes where -- I don't know whether they are forgeries as well, but at least where military people attended the meeting, if you never discussed military matters?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they were invited. I mean, when things were discussed. I mean, but if this has to do with giving tasks, objectives, no, never, no. And I mean these telephone communications, quite simply that makes no sense. Please, the Supreme Commander had communication with the president. You know, he was the commander. It wasn't the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you then explain to us where you said, I mean, when things were discussed in the presence of the military people attending the meeting, what kind of issues were then discussed if they were there, because you say it was not military matters. But what, then, was discussed in their presence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certain figures there, you know, who were not at the top but they were from the Sarajevo region, they were fighters, maybe -- actually it was more that these people self-organised and they would come there, asking for some kind of assistance and they would attend. Sometimes they would invite the army commander. He was there also. It was more a conversation about problems in the military, in the army, and not in the sense of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what kind of problems? It's rather vague in your answer. What kind of problems are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, financing problems, crime and so on and so forth. I can't remember because I know that this question wasn't really that pronounced so I can't recall details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll leave it for a moment, and move to -- perhaps I'll come back to it at a later stage. No, first, one additional question. You explained that the document shown to you must be a forgery because it contains information which you said could never have been discussed, nor would such a meeting be composed of the three of you mentioned. Any other reason apart from [indiscernible]. One second.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And not just that. There are many things here. For example, the Herzegovina theatre. I think that was, let's say, at the end, maybe it was November. And then this here, Trbojevic, Milojevic, about borders. I don't recall this. Especially not then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. All the reasons you gave are reasons based on -- please. Are reasons based on the substance of the content of these minutes. Is there anything of another category that would make you conclude that this is a forgery?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't remember that there was a session of the Presidency then, when I resigned. You know, first of all I prepared myself to give up my post. There was no Presidency meeting or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd give me one second, please. Yes. I'll move on to another subject. Could you tell us a bit more about your personal relationship with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know Mr. Krajisnik before he came to the assembly, shortly before the war. This was in 1990. I didn't know him at all before that. Then I got to know him in a way, I got to know him better when I became a minister in the government. That's when we were acquainted. But throughout the period before, I didn't know him. All I knew about him was that he worked in a company, that he was an economist; in a company, the financial director in the firm and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I heard that he was of a patriarchal mind, that he worked in that environment and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think my --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A believer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question, my previous question might not have been translated. You said he was an economist in a company, the financial director in the firm and so on. In the firm. What firm did you mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the TAT Energoinvest enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said earlier I think you worked at Energoinvest in your --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I worked as a young economist for less than two years, and then I got my post at university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You never met him when you were working for, Energoinvest at the time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on because you elaborated how you got to know him, when you got to know him better. I was asking you about what your relationship was like.
