Was it a relationship of friendship? Was it at a distance? Was it as you described earlier that Mr. Krajisnik was close in his opinions to Mr. Karadzic? Could you tell us a bit more about the relationship in more substantial terms rather than when you met him, when you got to know him better?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a formal relationship with Krajisnik, official relationship. As for our relationship during the war, it was a working relationship, and our relations were pretty cool, and we were at a distance. Briefly, what I can say is that we had an official relationship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time you call it "cool." I wouldn't say that everyone I have a professional or an official relationship with, that it would be cool. What's the reason why you described it as cool? Was this -- I'm not going to suggest anything to you. Could you tell us why you use that expression?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used it for the simple reason that the government was marginalised, it was left out of things, and Mr. Krajisnik was the president of the assembly. According to some logic -- first of all, the president of the assembly -- actually, the assembly and its president should be in favour of a strong government. That would be in their interest, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that you say that "I didn't like his attitude which was not strongly supporting the government"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that sense I said that and I said in the beginning, too, if I may put it like that, I was bothered somewhat by Krajisnik's indiscriminate, uncritical relationship to Karadzic. I think that they were friends but I still think that his attitude should have been different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you now for the second time are referring to the relationship between Karadzic and Krajisnik, the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We heard some evidence describing a situation in the meetings of the five, as I call them, in which Karadzic and Krajisnik were very dominant, and the others playing a role, second-class role. Would you -- could you comment on what we heard in this respect, to what extent you share such a view, to what extent you think it does not accurately describe the situation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the Presidency, there was Biljana, I was there on one side. On the other side there were Karadzic, Krajisnik and Koljevic. I'm simply trying to say that Karadzic mostly relied on Krajisnik. That is my impression. And a little bit on Koljevic too. I don't know why. I assume it was because he was a large regional entity so he was important to him. But he relied on Krajisnik in any case. Was this because he was the president of the assembly or because he thought him to be exceptionally wise? I don't know. I'm just giving you my impressions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I'd like to move to another subject. At the 22nd session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which was held on the 23rd and the 24th of November 1992, you complained that the Minister of Justice, that is Momcilo Mandic, and the Minister of the Interior, that is Mico Stanisic, reported to the president of the republic and to the president of the assembly. If you'd like to look at it, you'll find that under tab 4 of this bundle. And let me just find the right page. I haven't found yet the page. One second, please. I will read it out to you slowly and I think you can find it on -- I'm a bit surprised by what I find on page 12, as a matter of fact, but -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I think you'll find it at page 12, approximately the middle of the page. I received a copy where I find a white empty space in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Once again the same issue we discussed before. There was revised translation of this session. I believe the document, at least in front of me which is a copy of that --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- is a pre-revised translation. I have here for the Court -- in any event, the witness will be looking, of course, at the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the original, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- B/C/S, but if it's useful to the Court, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see -- I do understand that there was a revised translation. Let me then just take care that I do not quote from the wrong translation. Do you have the revised English so that I can be certain that I'm not going to quote from --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'll hand up pages 10 through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if I heard some whispering about notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I may have notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm looking to see that that's not the case and it does not seem to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, I'm willing to read it. Otherwise I would invite to you slowly read the English but -- now I have to find it because it's a totally different layout. I'm a bit lost, unfortunately. I quote your words where you said, "If somebody else insists on appointments of certain ministers, then the gentleman, that person, needs to assume responsibility for the work of those ministers as well. So far, not a single member of state leadership did that. On the contrary, everybody says the government is responsible, the Prime Minister is responsible, orchestration is responsible, and when it comes to the legislature, when we are dealing with the Minister of Justice, the Minister of the Interior, they are not even members of the government. They don't attend government meetings. They meet with the president of the republic and the chairman of the assembly. Not a single one of them ever appeared before the people or on TV and said they were responsible for their work and what they were doing, thereby releasing the Prime Minister of any liability. That would be fair." My question to you is: What exactly happened that made you express these or to speak these words in this assembly meeting where, if I understood your words well, you say they are not functioning within the government, they do not give me any possibility to take responsibility because they are directly dealing with the -- well, with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. What had happened that caused you to speak these words?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I simply said at the beginning that I was for the rule of law, that there should be a functioning state based on rule of law, and you cannot have that without certain functions of the ministry for internal affairs, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Defence and so on. Simply, as far as I was concerned, those ministries were not functioning in a certain way. The Ministry of Defence had a minister whom the army did not want to accept. The minister for internal affairs and the justice minister did not attend meetings. They were most frequently down there, at the Presidency, conditionally speaking. Problems were piling up. I mentioned earlier that I insisted that if there were crimes, they had to be processed. Somebody had to establish that such and such and act was a crime. I don't know the law of the perhaps the military police, the army, the police, can cross certain lines, but I wasn't qualified to establish whether that was so or not. So I asked the ministries of police, defence and justice to deal with that. That's one thing. The other thing was the level of criminalisation. This was something that was also an aspect of the rule of law. There were some other things too. I did not want to create the impression that this is just what we were talking about; the context is broader. These were the people who had to implement the activities of the government but they happened to be down there all the time. And then it turned out, since I kept asking that they be replaced in a certain way, I wanted the party to make that possible, then it turned out that they were openly saying that the Prime Minister was fighting against the president of the republic, that the Prime Minister had a different concept, that the president had a -- acted in accordance with the concept of the rule of law but the other one was acting in a different way and had a different concept. In any way, they were down there, with Karadzic. I'm saying Karadzic because he symbolised those events, that circle. Why? Because the government was marginalised. Why? It was just the set of circumstances that just created this situation where the government was simply left outside of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, first part of your answer, you explained that it was more or less the same issue that you explained to us before, definition of crime, the -- how the military police, the police can cross certain lines. You said I wasn't qualified to establish whether that was so or not. And then one line further down, you say, "The other thing was the level of criminalisation." Could you explain to us what you meant by that sentence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a bit earlier, I said it was possible for the border to be crossed. I mean I'm speaking in the conditional. That is why I wanted these two ministries to function. As for this question of criminalisation, you know ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean -- what were you referring to specifically when you said the level of criminalisation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was looting, simply put. Property was being alienated. Companies were being misused. Goods were crossing the border without the relevant documents. Resources were being wasted. Many questions. There was simply illegal action at work here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that crime committed by -- if such a distinction could be made -- crime committed by people of what nationality or ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "criminalisation" can also encompass that. All kinds of crimes, you understand, regardless of who committed them, whether it was committed by a member of this nation or that ethnic group or that ethnic group, whoever perpetrates a crime must be punished. We are talking about everything that can be considered a crime in a very broad sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let me ask you more specifically. Did you have specific concerns about, for example, Muslims committing looting in the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I primarily meant members of -- well, the Serb people, regardless of whether they were civilians or in the armed units, all of those who behave in an unlawful manner. I was not referring to the representatives of other ethnic groups, other nations. I was referring exclusively to the members of my own nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, could you tell us something about the relationship these two ministers, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Mandic had, with, to start with, Mr. Karadzic? Do you know anything about that? If so, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what their relationship was from earlier on, since when they had known each other and so on. In this period of time, while I was there, now, how long was this, seven months, while I was in government, well, I mean they were less in the government and they went to see him often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apart from the substance, you say they saw each other often but you have no further information about how close or how professional or --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I mean, I don't know. I cannot talk about that. I can assume that in part -- I mean, well, let's put it this way: It had to do with the actual office held because the Minister of Police, particular in conditions of war, right, well, he really does fall within the purview of those who are in charge of the army, and that was Karadzic, because according to one decision of the National Security Council, the army and everything that belongs to the armed forces was left to Karadzic. Others had nothing whatsoever to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now a similar question as far as the relationship between these two ministers and Mr. Krajisnik is concerned. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, I cannot say anything definite about that, except that Karadzic and Krajisnik had their offices right next door to each other, and in that building where they were, that's where these other people were, down there. I mean, I was informed or notified that they were down there for the most part. I told you that the government was 12 kilometres away, on the top of a mountain, 12 kilometres away from where Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic and Plavsic were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll move to another subject. At the 13th assembly session, which was held on the 24th of March, the government was tasked with creating, and I now quote from the minutes of that session, "tasked with creating an operational plan for assuming power, that is for establishing power in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and in particular in the field of internal affairs, National Defence and money transactions in all municipalities where we already have Serbian authorities and in those municipalities where we have only recently established Serbian municipalities." This was a quote from the stenographic record of this assembly session. If you'd like to have a look at it I'll give it to you but it is a quote, of course, a translated quote. Now, on the -- yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I don't know what assembly this is. As far as I can remember, there was no assembly -- I mean, of the Serb republic? Or perhaps of the Serb people? I mean, quite simply, I don't remember what assembly this was. But never mind. Please go on. I mean, where was this assembly held?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I couldn't immediately tell you. I have a list somewhere but I haven't brought it with me, but, if we know, I'll -- I hope we can tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was Pale, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was not near enough to the microphone; it was Pale, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was Pale, the 24th of March 1992. I quoted about the government being tasked with, and then I read what the government was tasked with. Now, on the 26th of April 1992, the Bosnian Serb government issued the so-called instructions for Serbian peoples, Crisis Staffs in municipalities. You would find that in the bundle you have in front of you, under tab 6. You see that document, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question would be whether these instructions, whether this document containing these instructions, was a response to the assembly request I just read to you, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, well, first of all, at this point in time that you are referring to, there was no government. There was just a Prime Minister-designate. There was no government. The government was established gradually. Perhaps only by the 1st of June or the end of May, there was a government of sorts, but at that time there was no government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secondly, who signed this? Who signed this document? I don't find this clear. I mean, this document -- I mean, this is a forgery too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What makes you conclude that this is a forgery? It appears, at least, to be unsigned. That leaves hardly any doubt.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because -- well, quite simply, because it refers to me and I see that I never came across this document, especially because certain prerogatives are given here, and I never dealt with this, you see. So it's a pure forgery. A set of instructions was sent to Crisis Staffs signed by Karadzic, and me, but meaning that they should be careful as to how they behave. I mean, if there is a conflict, that the conventions have to be borne in mind. I mean international rules and conventions. This was sent by fax at one point in time. And that would be obvious now. Whereas this was never sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pure -- pure forgery. That's what this document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any idea, where you say it's a forgery, who may have forged it? Do you have any knowledge of that? I'm not asking for any speculation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I cannot talk about that because obviously, well, this was done in a premeditated way. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it doesn't make much sense to ask further questions to you about this document so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please, don't. You see, I see the vocabulary used here, "hordes of robbers," "looters," and that is typical of the terminology used in the previous order, in the previous system, or "do not hinder trade," things like that. Quite simply, my own style of writing, this is not it. And I claim with full responsibility that this is a forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I then move on to my next subject. Earlier, when I asked you about an event on Koricanske Stijene, you started your answer, there was some confusion, where you thought that I was asking you for how -- whether you discussed or received information about collection centres. Could you tell us whether you received information about collection centres and what kind of information that was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We followed the work of these centres, and, well, we received some information and at any rate, I can tell you that these are reception centres, reception centres. Collection centres? Well, although in our own lexicon, the word camp is used alternatively, I mean, often this is done in a negativist way or rather it is read with a negative connotation. Well, these are purely reception centres, collection centres, for the population -- oh, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment. Could you tell us first of all -- no. Let's -- if you say these were reception centres, could you name some of them? I mean, otherwise, we are talking about a category rather than -- could you tell us what -- about what centres? And let's leave out for the time being the terminology. What centres you received information on? You said, "We followed the work of the centres." So could you please name a couple of them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trnopolje, further on -- well, Bileca, then out there in the Krajina, there was, I guess, Omarska and so on. I mean, I'm trying to tell you that more or less in every municipality there was such a reception centre, a bigger one or a smaller one, in order to protect the population of other ethnic backgrounds from possible retaliation or possible revanchism, especially in view of what happened in the first and Second World Wars and so on. I hope that you're aware of that, that this is an area with a great deal of national ethnic hatred, a lot of conflicts; this is such an unhappy country. And in the previous war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment. I can confirm to you that we heard a lot about that. So don't be concerned that we would not have received information on what we often heard Serbs feared would happen again. Now, how did you -- you mentioned Trnopolje, Bileca, Omarska. How did you receive this information? Were there reports?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, these were certain reports by the ministries in charge, the ministries in charge, primarily the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior. And then, well, when journalists started, well, debating this to a greater extent, then I asked for these centres to be visited and to compile a report in writing about that. And a certain team was established which went out there and toured these, well, collection centres, and then we saw, well, that there were some objections to. The different centres involved certain differences. Some were purely military ones, you see, like I mean, well, this Manjaca, it was a military centre before. I don't know much about this but I'm just telling you. I mean, I'm not really well-versed in this. It was only from this report that I saw, well, say, I mean, well, that somewhere out in the open, like Trnopolje, you see, that they were being visited by the International Red Cross. I mean, that's what's being written in some of these pieces of information, that they were being visited by charity organisations, even Muslim ones and Serb ones, and others, that some do not have a wire around them and so on, and that people are out in the open. I mean, it was even written that this was this open reception centre and so on. Well, in the case of others, you could see that there were even prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell us, you mentioned specifically, when you were talking about these reports, people being in the open, visits of the Red Cross, charity organisations visiting it. Was that about Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, believe me, I don't know the details. I'm only speaking from memory on the basis of this information, that that is what was written in that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember anything about reports you received on Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I mean, I don't remember any details. I just know that we concluded that conditions should be improved, that, well, quite simply, some people should be handed over to the military, well, generally speaking -- I mean, that they should be disbanded. I mean, as soon as we received this information, we reacted in that way. I mean, not much time went by and they were disbanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you talked about media. How did the information from the media come to you? I mean, did they come to your office? Did you see it when it was published? Did you see it on television? I mean, in what way did you receive what you just said was information by the media?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, well, this information, well, I mean, for the Minister of Information, or was this just a brief resume by the SRNA news agency? I mean, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did you receive that directly or was it through clippings prepared for the government or -- I mean, did you read the newspapers yourself? Did you read any magazines? Did you watch it to be shown on television? Or was it indirect?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a bit -- well, a bit indirectly but then also there was this information provided by the news agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I heard some things myself and then there were these brief reports of the news agency and then I asked the Minister of Information to explain this to me, to tell me what this was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you discuss this within the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, what? You mean the media?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The reporting in the media which was -- was the reporting alarming for you or -- you said you immediately took action.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost, and I've already said that and that's what I assert, there was a certain report or rather the Minister of Information spoke about that at a government session, and basically this was brought into the context of, well, sort of the world media were doing that at someone's intervention and so on and so forth, in order to cause a bombing of the Serb side and Serb positions. Those were more or less the comments about that. I mean, but I'm saying that independently of that and independently of such views, the government, as I've been saying, set up a commission, set up a working group, in order to tour the reception centres and to therefore receive better information about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this caused you -- may I first ask, was this discussed in the -- in any Presidency meetings as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, except that Karadzic was always sort of, well, linked to some information, media gave interviews, talked to them, but that this was discussed, no, I don't remember that. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take you -- do you remember when this media reporting became reason to discuss matters where you asked for further explanation to the ministry -- Minister of Information? Do you remember when that approximately was, in time? I'm trying to locate it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I think it was -- well, I don't know. Mid-summer. Now, when was this? Say, the end of July or August maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to take you for a couple of minutes until we have a break, take you back in time a little bit. According to the minutes of the government meeting on the 24th of May, that's far before the time you just mentioned, teams of ministers were formed for on-site investigations in municipalities and would prepare reports and suggest measures to be undertaken. And let me just see whether I've -- yes. I'm consulting my staff because there was a translation issue in relation to this document. Yes. So I just told you then that on the 24th of May, teams of ministers were formed for on-site investigations in municipalities - for the parties I'm referring to P65, tab 139 - and would prepare reports and suggest measures to be undertaken. Now, if you'd like to read it, Mr. Djeric, you would find it in tab 7. According to the minutes from the government meeting on the 29th of May, that is five days later, the ministers should and I now quote from tab 8, which is P65, tab 140 -- so I'm now at the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 24th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one is --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm so sorry. You are referring to the record of the 24th of May? Are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that this hasn't been signed either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's good that you draw our attention to it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I used to sign records, all of them, minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- but if we look at the content, you could tell us whether this reflects what was discussed so whether it's just a document which -- of which we received an unsigned version --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean these minutes? You mean the minutes of the 24th of May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to look at the content first, and of course it's good that you draw our attention to the fact that it's not signed, whatever that would mean under the present circumstances. But in the document --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These minutes simply are a forgery. They are not authentic. And you can see it was agreed that the president of the Assembly of the Serbian People, Momcilo Krajisnik, organises a meeting. The government did not have the authority of tasking Krajisnik, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you are now referring to what specific portion, Mr. Djeric, so that I'm able to follow you? Under 3?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: ED 31, minutes of the 24th of May. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say that this is a forgery because that could not have taken place, that it has been agreed that Mr. Krajisnik should set up a meeting, because you were not in a position to -- not to order him to do so or not to --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not issue him with a task. I could not entrust anything to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's clear. Nevertheless, I'd like to -- I quoted, as a matter of fact, but it's good that you draw our attention to your opinion that this is a forgery. I just read a portion to you that is -- that these minutes say that teams of ministers were formed for on-site investigations in municipalities and would prepare reports and suggest measures to be undertaken. Mr. Djeric, do you remember, so apart from these minutes, whether ever a decision was taken that teams of ministers would be formed for on-site investigations in municipalities and prepare reports? So apart from --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the usual procedure in the government to entrust a certain ministry or a number of ministries with visiting and then informing the government about certain questions. This was our practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially if it was within their responsibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to inform us how the law was operating on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then take you to the minutes of the government meeting on the 29th of May? And perhaps it's good to ask you whether you consider them to be -- they are unsigned. You find them under tab 8, whether you consider them to be a forgery as well. Yes. There we read that -- which ministers are responsible for the visits to what municipalities, and then I quote, "In the course of these visits, they should talk to the Crisis Staffs, take note of the situation, by all means visit the front, make contact with the soldiers, and prepare a report about it for the government."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say that? Ah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will assist you. You see that Mr. Trbojevic and Mr. Ostojic should go to Vogosca and Ilijas and Mr. Lajic and Zukovic should go to Stari Grad and Centar. Have you found that? You can find it under 1 at the very end. You found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us why the ministers, so Mr. Trbojevic and Ostojic for Vogosca and Ilijas, and Mr. Lajic and Zukovic for Stari Grad and Centar, why they were tasked with these kind of visits, including visiting the front, make contact with soldiers, then prepare a report for the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, this is not the front in the sense that it is usually understood. This is just an organised people, people who were in their homes, defending their homes, their hearths and so on. So we are talking about self-organised people affected by war, and that is why the government asked these people to go and visit them, to see there was some kind of line of conflict there, where the operations were. So we are talking about self-organised people here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether these ministers made these visits?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure. I don't know if they were there, if they went. I don't know. But the practice was to go see those people -- see the population actually, because I'm reminding you, the army, the Main Staff, was appointed on the 12th of May, so practically it was the -- just self-organised people. So it's very far from being an army in the proper sense, you understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand your answer. We'll have a break at this moment, 20 minutes. We'll resume at 5.30 -- at 6.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, during the fifth session of the Presidency, you'll find the minutes, or at least brief notes, under tab 1. It is a meeting held on the 10th of June 1992 and you are reported in this minutes as being present. The government is tasked to submit a report on prisoners with proposed measures. Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, this is also the subject, in fact, of a recent e-mail. I lap to have the correct translation provided by the translation unit and the court officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps, Mr. Djeric, would you please listen carefully to the correct translation of what I just read? Perhaps you first of all look at the version in your own language because you're not dependent on any -- on any translation, since you have the original in front of you, or at least the B/C/S version. Mr. Tieger would you please read slowly how the line is translated in the newest version?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That "the government submit a report on prisoners, with proposed measures."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's approximately what was in mine because I discussed the matter with the staff and asked to have the newest translation to -- okay. So therefore, the government is given the task to submit a report on prisoners, with proposed measures. Could you tell us whether the government ever reported to the Presidency or any other body on the situation of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this assignment at all, because if someone was assigned to this, then it could have been the Ministry of Justice only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Presidency session minutes say that it would be the government. Have you found it in the original? It's at the -- almost at the very end.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that that is what is written here but I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, whether or not you recall that, do you remember whether ever a government report was addressed to the Presidency or any other body on the situation of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. That's why I said just now I don't know whether the Minister of Justice, who spent all of his time with the president, was the line that was used. I don't recall whether it went along that line perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I put to you a document. And for the parties, I'm referring now to P583, tab 20, of which I understand a copy is prepared. Yes. Oh, that's an extra one. It should be found in the bundle under "extra one," which are the minutes of the 25th session of the Bosnian Serb government, 10th of June, that's the same date as the previous document, item 7, Mr. Djeric, where the Minister of Justice is tasked with reporting on present conditions and specifically contacting the managers of Panorama, Buducnost, and Kikinda. Does that refresh your memory in any way as to reporting on prison conditions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm not seeing the word conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I again let me just have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I see the word somewhere on the page but I don't see it in that context directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should -- it was a short version. I'll read the whole of it to Mr. Djeric. "That the Ministry of Justice should make a report about prisoners. This report should pay special attention on treatment of civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera. The report would be considered by the government after which it would be submitted to the Presidency of the republic." Let's leave it to that and leave out the following portion. Does this refresh your memory where it seems that the Minister of Justice is tasked with preparing a report, specifically to be later then sent to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the details, I don't, but that's why I intervened earlier, because if anything was there, it could only have been addressed to the Ministry of Justice and not to the government. My whole problem, and I keep underlining this, was the problem in communication with the Minister of Justice, because if he was being tasked to do things, then he also had to implement these tasks. He had to carry them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, shortly after that, we find in the minutes of the 28th session of the Bosnian Serb government, 15th of June 1992, we find that in item 10, a working group is created consisting of Mr. Djeric, Mr. Trbojevic, Mr. Kalinic, Mr. Subotic, and finally Mr. Mandic to consider all aspects of the prisoner exchange programme. Do you have any recollection of such a working group being formed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think that that is correct, that the minutes are correct, because -- it's not correct simply because the Prime Minister would not take part in something like this. Usually, when teams were being formed for certain assignments, then that could have been the Deputy Prime Minister, who was a lawyer, and certain ministers, from the justice ministry, from the MUP or the Defence Ministry and so on. The Prime Minister was not the one to be dealing with these questions. I think that something here is not quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was such a working --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Perhaps I could have been tasked with visiting Krajina, in the political sense and so on, but as for these questions, I'm sure that I would not be the one to deal with them, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you do not remember that such a -- you do not remember that such a working group was formed or that you took part in it, is that -- or do you --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The working group was formed. I said earlier that the government did form it. I kept trying to establish rule of law on the ground. We were asking for a state of rule of law to be set up. I just want to remind you that these party organs had ruled for a long time so it was very difficult for the rule of law to come into being. So I insisted on that and exposed myself to various unpleasant things, and I strived to bring the laws into operation, to implement them. So I'm just asking who could that have been? Earlier, when you were asking me about visiting the municipality, I really don't remember specifically whether that team was in Vogosca or so on. I don't remember that. But it was my practice to send teams to visit the population that was self-organised because they needed food, and other articles that were essential for their everyday life, and we were trying to be present in those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let me take you back because we have these 10th of June minutes, and could you please have a look at the original? Is that your signature which we find at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be absolutely 100 per cent certain as to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That it is, you would say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think actually that it is. There is something. It does resemble it, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot state that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- okay. I take you back to that meeting and again read a specific portion of the task given to the Ministry of Justice, it reads that, "The Ministry of Justice should make a report about prisoners." That's how it starts. Then it says, "This report should pay special attention on treatment of civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera." Could you explain the two categories to us, two categories mentioned in a report about prisoners; that is, 1, civilian population, and, 2, prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, and I cannot give you a precise classification of what at the time was civilian population and what was a prisoner of war. I assume that those persons who had entered the ranks of armed conflict and who carried weapons and acted against the armed forces of the armed -- of the Serbian people, that they would be considered prisoners of war. I assume again, as I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You've not explained the second category, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a question of regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the second category, I'd like to -- you've explained to us what you understood, not being a lawyer, what were prisoners of war, but I asked for two categories, the one, prisoner of war, and the other, one civilian population.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I said -- I said that I don't -- not that I think but that I assume that the difference is in the fact that who carried weapons and fought against the armed forces of Republika Srpska and those who did not. The people who did not bear weapons and did not participate in the fighting, I assume that that was the civilian population and the others were prisoners. I assume that you're asking me something that is not something that I am well-versed in. I can -- it's not my profession. I mean, I can just tell you in general. I mean, it's a question of what the regulations are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it suggests, the wording suggest that among prisoners you would find a category, prisoners of war, and a category described as civilian population. I'm seeking your explanation on how civilian population would be among a group which is called prisoners.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm simply starting from the fact that all this was done within the relevant regulations by the Ministry of Justice and that these categories existed. What they stood for, I really cannot speak about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if I ask you, write a report about prisoners, and pay specific attention on how civilian population is treated and pay specific attention to prisoners of war, would that not suggest that among prisoners there was a category described as civilian population?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but it seems more natural to me, when you put it like that, that in the civilian population there were certain persons identified who bore weapons, participated in the fighting and so on but I really cannot speak about that. These are things that I really didn't deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The government tasked the Ministry of Justice to report about it, isn't it? And the government specified the specific points which would need attention.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The government set off from certain regulations in this particular field, and according to the regulations, you know who is a civilian, who is a prisoner of war, and the Ministry of Justice was supposed to submit a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Djeric, I move a little bit further on. Exchange of prisoners. What would that mean? You said a working group was formed, apart from whether you were involved in that. What did you understand by exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One side and the other captured persons during the fighting, soldiers, and then they would exchange them. I cannot be more specific about that because I wasn't involved in those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exchange of prisoners had nothing to do with the exchange of civilians who were in prisons or were detained?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really am unable -- well, the task here is quite clear, that the ministry should prepare the question of the civilian population, prisoners of war and so on, to create rule of law, to respect rule of law, and to make sure that suitable treatment is being respected or applied. They -- these things were something that was conducted by certain groups, by the military, the Ministry of Internal Affairs. They were involved in these exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you aware of whether the Bosnian Serb Presidency, or in your contacts with the Bosnian Serb Presidency, that there was awareness that they learned about the detention of Muslim or Croat civilians in areas under Bosnian Serb control?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of problems there. I think that the leadership didn't have the real information about that. For a long time, the Crisis Staffs were in charge, the local factor was in charge down there, and they didn't report back or inform anyone about that. We were cut off for a long time, physically. Information-wise. In different ways, we were not able to reach certain points, certain areas, certain municipalities, and so on. So that awareness about these problems, in the beginning, was totally -- there was just no way to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say in the beginning. When did such an awareness, that is awareness about detention of Muslim and Croat -- Muslim or Croat civilians in areas under Bosnian Serb control, you said in the beginning they were not aware. When did they become aware of such detention?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about others. I'm just speaking for myself. I found out more about it only -- or rather, in relation to these -- these camps and so on, certain information that the government received, this was already the month of September. That's when I found out about it. Before that, I had no idea that there were such things, except in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except in this option that I was talking about, the collection centres or the reception centres. These reception centres were organised in municipalities by the local authorities to protect the -- the other population, until the crisis blew over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you form an opinion when this reporting started? This Chamber received evidence that it was on the 6th of August that CNN reported on Omarska. Did you know actually what happened in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. I didn't know. I didn't know. And you see there was constant activity. The government was sending teams to prepare information so that we would be updated. Many things went on without the knowledge of the government, because of the pronounced strength of the local factor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do you know now, at this very moment, what actually happened in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, even at this point, right now, I don't know much about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you in a position to almost immediately - that means within one or two days - to deny that the reporting had at least some truth in it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which reporting, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The CNN reporting. You just referred to the media. Were you in a position to state whether the reporting was true or was not true, almost immediately after this reporting took place?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for me, that was simply something that was ultimately indicative and that's how I behaved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Indicative of what, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I simply -- something was happening, something was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you take it seriously, this reporting? Did you accept that it could -- could be true or at least partially be true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I proceeded from the premise that there could be something, and that is the attitude I took to that afterwards. I mean, not only then but before that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I present to you -- and I'll finish in a couple of minutes. May I present to you P1248? Have the parties received copies of it? It's -- yes. Mr. Djeric, could you please indicate where in this document, which appears to be, but if I'm wrong, please correct me, a press release from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina government, where the government expresses that the reports are taken seriously and that, as you said, the reporting was indicative and that something was happening, something was going on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, well, I don't know who wrote this, because -- I mean, I don't know who made this on behalf of the government. I mean, let's first clear that up, because it was customary there, often, that this term, "the government" would be launched and I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you say that this was -- do you dispute that this was a government press release or do you say may have been issued but I was not aware? I mean, what's exactly your situation, your position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is quite simply that if the government had stated this, then it would have to be signed by the Prime Minister, and if it was released by I don't know who, then some other factor would have to sign this. One has to know if it's the Presidency, then it's the Presidency. If it's the Ministry of Information then the Ministry of Information. You see, if it's the government, then -- well, it would have to bear my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you point at any public statement you made at that time which would reflect what you just told us, that the reporting was indicative and something was happening, something was going on? Did you ever make a public statement in that respect?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I was not involved in this matter. I mean, well, you see, I mean, as for myself, I did practically, well, everything that on the groundworking groups should go there and this should be visited. That's what matters, as far as I'm concerned. I established working groups to tour the area and to do whatever was possible. So possibly if there were some negative or adverse sides to this, then that should be redressed. That is where I saw my role, not in statements. I made very few statements, if I made any statements. And if I made any statements they were along the lines of, well, equality in resolving conflicts. I mean, well, within some rules that suited all three sides. So, I proceeded from the premise that once again the area should be toured and that the situation should be recorded as it was, fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. We'll finish for the day, Mr. Djeric. Could we ask Madam Usher to escort Mr. Djeric out of the courtroom but not until after I instructed you, as I did yesterday, Mr. Djeric, that you should not speak to anyone about the testimony already given or still about to be given. And we would like to see you back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in this same courtroom. Yes. Madam Usher could you please escort Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I note that the parties always would like to know how we use our time further on. The Chamber expects that it would not need more than one hour tomorrow. And then the remaining time the Chamber would like to hear from the parties how much time they would like to have for the time remaining, and that would be the remainder of Thursday and we have planned that on Friday, although perhaps not fully until 7.00, but at least most of a normal session could be spent on the examination of Mr. Djeric. So I'd like to know from the parties, perhaps by tomorrow, how much time, keeping in mind how much time is approximately available, that is altogether, I would, say some five to six hours. Yes. Then we will adjourn to tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of July, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
